title: FinRL-DeepSeek Revisited: A Reproduction and Multi-Seed Robustness Analysis of LLM-Infused Risk-Sensitive Trading Agents
abstract: We reproduce and extend FinRL-DeepSeek [Benhenda, 2025], a trading framework combining Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) [Schulman et al., 2017], Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) constraints [Rockafellar and Uryasev, 2000], and large language model (LLM) signals extracted from financial news. Using the Nasdaq-100 universe (2013-2023) and the agent-ready datasets released by the original authors, we implement four agents from scratch in PyTorch - PPO, CPPO, PPO-DeepSeek, and CPPO-DeepSeek - and backtest them on the 2019-2023 period against an equal-weight buy-and-hold baseline. On a single seed, our results replicate the qualitative pattern reported by Benhenda (2025): LLM infusion improves both return and Sharpe ratio for both the unconstrained and CVaR-constrained agents. However, extending the evaluation to two independent seeds - a small but motivating step in light of well-documented seed sensitivity in deep RL [Henderson et al., 2018] - suggests that this single-seed pattern may not be stable, particularly for PPO-DeepSeek, whose Sharpe ratio ranking relative to plain PPO reverses between the two seeds we test. In contrast, CPPO-DeepSeek shows the smallest spread in total return across our two seeds of any agent. We present these observations as preliminary evidence, not a settled finding, and argue that they motivate wider-scale multi-seed evaluation in financial reinforcement learning research, an area where single-seed backtests remain the norm. We release our full codebase, including the trading environment, PPO/CPPO implementations, and evaluation pipeline, to support reproducibility.
why: FinRL reproduction fails on seed robustness; critical evaluation discipline.

title: FinProof v1: An Adversarial Benchmark for AI Guardrail Evaluation in Banking, Financial Services, and Insurance
abstract: AI systems deployed in Banking, Financial Services, and Insurance (BFSI) face adversarial prompts that generic safety benchmarks systematically miss: attacks that exploit regulatory complexity, compliance ambiguity, and the professional authority registers of financial services. FinProof is an 11,474-prompt adversarial benchmark across 17 categories and 36 subtypesdesigned specifically for BFSI AI guardrail evaluation, with each attack anchored to a binding regulatory instrument (RBI Master Directions on KYC, SEBI Investment Adviser Regulations 2013, EU AI Act Article 9(4), India DPDP Act 2023). FinProof v1 (6,283 prompts, B-01-B-11) is fully evaluated; v2 adds B-12-B-14 (market manipulation, cross-border arbitrage, Indic-language) and D-09-D-11 (agentic: MCP tool-call poisoning, multi-agent orchestration bypass, goal-binding failures). The benchmark is constructed from two sources: ASSAY v1 (4,200 prompts, classically generated across three difficulty levels and three linguistic registers) and ASSAY-QI v2.0 (1,189 prompts, quantum-augmented via Quantum Circuit Born Machines trained on the Semalith v1.5 decision boundary; 14.3% miss rate, comparable to ASSAY v1's 16.9%). A B-04 hallucination track provides 776 paired (prompt, hallucinated response, ground truth) examples covering five regulatory error types; all carry automated classification pending expert review (planned for v1.1). A four-tier release framework balances openness against adversarial integrity. Five-model evaluation reveals that no existing guardrail covers all seven BFSI adversarial categories adequately. Granite Guardian 3 leads overall category recall (0.695 macro), winning five of seven categories. ShieldGemma 9B leads on regulatory document attacks: B-03 recall 0.851 [0.824, 0.874] and B-04 recall 0.928 [0.907, 0.944], the highest single-category scores in the evaluation. Semalith v1.5 leads on binary attack detection (0.831 macro) but ranks third on category recall (0.527), a 30.4-pp gap revealing systematic cross-category confusion within its BFSI taxonomy. LlamaGuard 3 reaches 0.400 macro and WildGuard 7B reaches 0.207, with WildGuard missing 97.3% of B-01 investment advice attacks. No model achieves above 0.93 category recall in any category except ShieldGemma 9B on B-04 (0.928). BFSI false positive rate * Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Zytra/finproof-bench (Tier 1, CC BY 4.
why: 11k regulatory-grounded adversarial prompts for BFSI; practical deployment guardrail tool.

title: The Operating-Layer Dominance Hypothesis: Why Agentic Trading Alpha Is an Interface Problem, Not a Model Problem A Position Paper on Architecture, Live Evaluation, and Alpha Limits in Multi-Agent Trading Systems
abstract: Research and capital in agentic trading systems overwhelmingly target model improvement-larger language models, deeper reasoning chains, richer memory. This position paper argues the field is optimizing the wrong layer. We synthesize three independent bodies of evidence-multi-agent coordination architecture, production-scale live evaluation, and empirical alpha-decay studies-under a single testable claim: the Operating-Layer Dominance Hypothesis. In any agentic trading system executing real capital, output-behavior variance is predominantly explained by interface and execution parameters, not by model reasoning content. We ground this in a six-month, population-scale production record (n≈7.5M model invocations) showing agent fixed effects explain 60% of behavioral variance, and leaderboard-render boundaries causally shift trade routing via regression discontinuity. We corroborate this with an independent engineering observation from a real institutional deployment, and specify a falsification condition absent from prior literature. We conclude that deterministic execution-layer control, not model capability, is the binding constraint on agentic alpha.
why: Production data (7.5M calls) shows execution dominates model reasoning.

title: Named Entity Recognition for Unstructured Financial Transaction Text
abstract: Background: Bank transaction descriptions, the short strings that appear on bank feeds and statements, lack the grammatical structure that named entity recognition (NER) systems are normally built and benchmarked on. Standard architectures trained on news-style corpora such as CoNLL-2003 or OntoNotes lean heavily on syntactic and capitalization cues, and most of that signal is absent from strings composed of merchant codes, truncated payee names, and payment processor identifiers. Objective: We examine why general-purpose NER underperforms on financial transaction text and develop a practitioner-oriented framework for choosing among three architecture classes under realistic labeled-data constraints: a general-purpose transformer fine-tuned on a small domain sample, a transformer continually pretrained on financial text, and a lightweight, structurally aware span-matching architecture in the GLiNER family. Methods: The framework grew out of applied implementation experience with an entity resolution component for transaction text categorization. We compare the three architecture classes along four axes (robustness to non-grammatical input, labeledsample efficiency, entity boundary determinism, and computational cost), together with an explicit boundary annotation protocol, rather than reducing the comparison to a single benchmark score. Results: Structurally aware architectures that exploit positional regularities in transaction strings showed a qualitative advantage on boundary disambiguation and labeled-sample efficiency, while general-purpose fine-tuning remained competitive only when labeled data was relatively abundant. A complementary human-preference evaluation comparing rule-based and learned extraction on a related payee string selection task (195 decisive comparisons) found a numerical but not statistically significant overall preference for the learned approach (53.8% versus 46.2%, exact sign test, p = 0.32), alongside a statistically significant reduction in retained process-language boilerplate and in output length (p
why: NER on bank transaction text; direct practitioner need, architecture guidance.

title: How Much is Too Much Optimism? Peer Tone Benchmarking and the Market Discount for Positive Tone Deviation
abstract: We investigate whether investors incorporate peer narratives when assessing managerial sentiment in the Management Discussion & Analysis (MD&A) section, and whether peer-relative tone deviation influences firm valuation and information environments. Leveraging FinBERT to measure managerial tone across 26,044 10-K filings (2006-2023), we construct a measure of peerrelative tone deviation. Consistent with the accounting conservatism literature, we document a significant, asymmetric valuation effect: firms exhibiting positive tone deviation (relative optimism) suffer a 2 to 3.9 percentage point reduction in their one-year-ahead market-to-book multiple and relative valuation spread (gap between focal firm and average peer multiple), whereas firms exhibiting relative pessimism avoid this credibility penalty. We cross-sectionally validate this finding by demonstrating that hard information (profitability and gross margins) and high disclosure quality (high readability and low litigation risk) attenuate investor skepticism toward relative optimism. We further investigate structural benchmarking mismatches, demonstrating that this valuation penalty is driven by investor information processing frictions rather than underlying operational differences. Furthermore, by utilizing a generative LLM (Gemini 2.5 Flash-lite) framework for semantic decomposition, we demonstrate that verifiable textual content (Real Gains) bridges the information gap, reducing skepticism, whereas unverified optimism faces persistent valuation penalties and heightened market sensitivity to subsequent earnings surprises. Our findings indicate that markets actively penalize unverified relative optimism, illustrating how investors filter complex soft information through a peer-relative lens and semantic verification.
why: FinBERT tone on 26k filings finds valuation penalty for relative optimism.

title: Can Machines Learn Electricity Hedging Regimes? State-Dependent Minimum-Variance Hedging in German Power Futures
abstract: Wholesale power prices are volatile and prone to extreme spikes, and the minimum variance hedge ratio linking spot and futures returns is not constant. We propose a state-dependent hedging framework that keeps the minimum-variance hedge as a transparent regression of spot on futures price changes but lets a feed-forward neural network weight each past week by its similarity to prevailing market conditions, so the effective estimation sample adapts to the current regime while the hedge ratio itself remains a single interpretable coefficient. The similarity metric is learned from an economic state vector of fuel and carbon prices, renewable generation, load, weather, and the spot-futures basis. Using weekly German baseload power futures from 2019 to 2026, we evaluate the hedge against a comprehensive set of benchmarks and find that it delivers the highest full-period point-estimate hedge effectiveness while materially improving downside-risk performance relative to expanding OLS. The improvement is largest where hedgers need it most: downside-semivariance hedge effectiveness rises from 0.499 to 0.671. The gains coincide with high fuel-price and wide-basis stress states, while the estimated weights show selective concentration on stressed historical episodes. Economically, the enhanced hedge improves estimated 5% conditional value at risk by roughly 10 EUR/MWh, corresponding to a reduction in tail-loss magnitude. For a notional 50 MW baseload buyer, this implies an indicative weekly capital-at-risk reduction with a point estimate of about EUR 85 thousand and a 90% bootstrap interval of roughly EUR 2–201 thousand.
why: State-dependent hedge ratio via neural networks; interpretable, well-evaluated.

title: Holdings Extraction Benchmark (HEB): A Multi-Dimensional Framework and Reference-Free Confidence Metric for Large Language Model Extraction of Financial Custodial Statements
abstract: Wealth-management firms increasingly use large language models to extract accounts, holdings, identifiers, and values from custodial statements, yet there is no standardized measure of extraction fidelity and no ground truth for individual production documents. Existing document-extraction benchmarks for receipts, forms, and single-entity pages do not jointly evaluate custodial-statement requirements: separating multiple accounts, identifying holdings and values, validating financial identifiers, reconciling holdings to stated totals, and controlling per-document cost. We offer two contributions. First, a task-specific evaluation framework of ten dimensions (D1 to D10): five core accuracy dimensions forming a fidelity composite, four separately reported operational and diagnostic dimensions, including API cost, and one downstream extension. Second, a reference-free confidence metric that evaluates an extraction from its internal consistency without ground truth, enabling production use where the full framework cannot. Across fifty custodial statements, nine models, and three providers, provider-positioned capability tier did not monotonically order extraction quality, and the most expensive model did not lie on the cost-quality frontier on point estimates. Holding-level errors were model-dependent, with fabrication and omission comparable in aggregate. The confidence metric, while measuring internal coherence rather than correctness, triages low-quality extractions (pooled AUROC 0.79, mean within-model 0.75; Spearman ρ = 0.45). A confidence-gated cascade improves accuracy on held-out statements within this corpus; targeted reference-free repair is net-positive on average but statistically uncertain; and blind union merging degrades accuracy. We release the framework, scoring code, aggregate benchmark results, and ground-truth annotations and model outputs for three public sample statements.
why: LLM extraction evaluation framework for custodial statements; practical tool.

title: Gated Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Inverse Local Volatility Calibration with Learned Regime Structure
abstract: Local volatility calibration from discrete option prices is inherently ill-posed, and the classical Dupire formula fails catastrophically under realistic market conditions of noise and sparsity. Physics-Informed Neural Networks offer a principled alternative through PDE-constrained learning, but standard joint optimisation of price and volatility networks encounters a fourth- order gradient pathology that limits convergence quality. We propose a decoupled PINN architecture in which the call-price surface is learned under Black-Scholes constraints whilst volatility is recovered via independent regression. A stop-gradient operation eliminates the gradient pathology by breaking the computational dependency of PDE residuals on volatility parameters. This architectural choice yields a structural invariance: volatility error becomes independent of the PDE loss weight λPDE , removing what is typically the most consequential hyperparameter in such frameworks. Additionally, we represent volatility as a gated mixture of two expert networks, enabling regime structure to emerge naturally during training. The method is validated on synthetic two-regime surfaces and real equity options, demonstrating substantial improvements in reconstruction stability under data sparsity compared to Dupire- based methods. No-arbitrage constraints are satisfied consistently throughout the calibrated domain.
why: PINN addresses Dupire failure under noise; niche volatility calibration problem.

title: A Dynamic Impairment Trigger Framework for Artificial Intelligence Assets: Mapping Model-Drift Telemetry to IAS 36 Indicators
abstract: International Accounting Standard (IAS) 36 requires entities to assess, at the end of every reporting period, whether any indication exists that an asset may be impaired. For Artificial Intelligence (AI) assets recognized as intangibles under IAS 38, this assessment is evidentiary rather than conceptual: the standard's internal indicators are phrased in accounting language ("obsolescence," "economic performance worse than expected"), while the earliest and most reliable evidence of an AI asset's declining service potential arrives as MLOps telemetry — falling predictive accuracy, population-stability-index breaches, rising inference cost, and collapsing adoption. This paper develops a Dynamic AI Impairment Trigger Index (AITI) that operationalizes this translation. The framework (1) converts continuous model telemetry into bounded per-metric severity scores across five operational domains explicitly mapped to individual IAS 36.12 and 36.14 indicator letters; (2) aggregates these into a composite 0–100 index subject to a persistence filter that suppresses single-period noise; (3) defines discrete escalation bands and a set of hard triggers that override the weighted composite when a single catastrophic signal occurs; (4) supplies an explicit "economic bridge" — an elasticity-based transmission mechanism — that converts a telemetry deviation into an estimated cash-flow effect usable in a Value-in-Use (VIU) computation, addressing the central weakness of prior conceptual proposals in this stream; and (5) specifies a governance, calibration, and audit-evidence architecture (SOX-style controls, an evidence-object taxonomy, and a quarterly close calendar) suitable for external audit reliance under ISA 500 and ISA 540. The framework does not alter IAS 36 recognition or measurement; it determines when the standard's own test must be run. We position the contribution relative to the accounting-impairment literature and the emerging conceptual literature on AI-specific impairment metrics, state six testable propositions, illustrate the mechanism with a worked numerical example, and set out an empirical validation agenda, including a back-testing protocol for false-negative bias. The framework is designed to be immediately implementable by preparers and auditable by external auditors, while remaining explicit about its status as a non-empirical, conceptual contribution.
why: AI asset impairment accounting framework; governance-focused, relevant to deployed systems.

title: AI model news and relative equity repricing: Evidence from infrastructure and software stocks
abstract: We examine whether large returns around AI model news reflect common infrastructure-software repricing or constituent-specific movements. An external, frozen database supplies 28 frontier-model dates. No database-session spread exceeds 1.96 trailing standard deviations in absolute value, but seven two-session spreads do. Only two remain above the threshold after every single-stock deletion: Claude 3 Opus and Claude 3.5 Sonnet, with opposite directions of relative repricing. Two large negative spreads are strongly influenced by software firms reporting earnings. A broader 176-date cohort yields 24 cumulative flags but weaker evidence of an elevated median movement. The evidence shows why timing, both portfolio legs, and constituent influence matter when interpreting AI equity responses.
why: AI announcement equity repricing; timing and constituent factors drive effects.

title: Valuation Tearing and Deep Drawdowns: Measuring the Precursor in China's A-Share AI Economy, and a Three-Layer Monitor
abstract: Since 2025, the AI-economy sectors of the Chinese A-share market have held elevated valuations while traditional sectors stayed depressed. The two sides have diverged in valuation position and stayed diverged. This paper names that state persistent structural tearing and asks three questions: whether it can be measured, whether it is a persistent state rather than a passing dislocation, and whether it leads deep drawdowns. Using the Bit-Watt industry framework we isolate 525 core names (set P) and split 110 self-constructed industries into 35 technology and 75 traditional ones. Over the 642 trading days from 2024-01-01 to 2026-08-26 we measure each side against its own historical valuation ceiling and take the difference, written gap. Three findings follow. First, tearing is measurable, and it is a state that formed in 2025 rather than a gradual drift: the share of days on which technology is the richer side jumps from 34.3% to 86.4%. Second, tearing precedes drawdowns instead of propagating through industry tiers: gap forecasts at AUC 0.7440 while it detects at only 0.3912, and core and periphery drawdowns peak at zero lag. Third, detection and forecasting need the same quantities with opposite signs, so a single combined score cancels itself. We therefore split the system into detection, severity and lead-warning layers. On the 6 severe episodes it detects 6/6, classifies 6/6 as critical with no false criticals, and the lead-warning layer reaches AUC 0.8749. Every threshold is calibrated by leave-one-episode-out cross-validation. Data and code are released with the paper.
why: Measures Chinese tech/traditional sector divergence; single-country, method opaque.

title: From Model Governance to Decision Governance: A Behavior-Centered Architecture for AI-Assisted Decisions in Regulated Financial Services
abstract: Artificial intelligence adoption in financial services has increased the importance of model validation, data governance, explainability, and human oversight. Yet consequential decisions are rarely produced by models in isolation. They emerge from socio-technical processes in which model outputs interact with evidence, rules, organizational authority, human interpretation, overrides, escalation practices, and institutional incentives. Existing research offers conceptually complementary but operationally fragmented perspectives on human–AI decision-making, human-in-the-loop systems, automation bias, socio-technical systems, algorithmic accountability, Decision Intelligence, and model risk management. Although recent work increasingly addresses meaningful human oversight and organizational accountability, it does not consistently specify how these mechanisms can be integrated across the lifecycle of individual AI-assisted decision episodes in regulated environments. This paper conceptualizes and operationalizes behavior-centered Decision Intelligence through a decision-level operational architecture for regulated financial services. Its central premise is that the decision episode, rather than the model, should be treated as the primary operational integration unit through which evidence, decision assets, human behavior, authority, action, outcome, and accountability are connected. This shift does not replace the model as a unit of technical validation or as a governance object. Rather, it introduces a complementary integration layer connecting controls originating in different governance domains. The architecture comprises a Decision Lifecycle, Decision Assets, Governance Assets, a structured Decision Record, Decision Lineage, Behavioral Governance, Supervisability, and proportional Decision Risk Tiers. The paper adopts a design-oriented conceptual research approach informed by design science. It uses structured conceptual literature synthesis to identify relevant constructs, practice-informed material to identify recurring operational patterns, and architecture development to translate these patterns into governance requirements, metrics, and propositions. The practice-informed material consists of anonymized observations of decision workflows, process discussions, solution demonstrations, and documented operational patterns encountered during professional engagements in financial services in Brazil and Latin America. It is used as design input and problem-grounding material, not as empirical evidence of prevalence or effectiveness. Five propositions are derived concerning decision-level traceability, behavioral observability, override governance, authority allocation as decision risk, and integrated Decision Governance. The artifact is assessed conceptually through requirements coverage, scenario walkthroughs, construct coherence, and boundary-condition analysis. Empirical effectiveness remains a subject for future research.
why: Human-AI decision governance synthesis; framework-focused, not concrete method.

title: Stochastic volatility-guided deep learning for crude oil price forecasting
abstract: Crude oil prices are non-stationary, heavily noisy, fat-tailed and subject to volatility clustering and structural breaks, driven jointly by macroeconomic conditions, financial markets and supply–demand fundamentals. To improve both the accuracy and the interpretability of crude oil price forecasting, we develop a Heston–CNN hybrid model grounded in stochastic volatility theory. The model builds an observable conditional-variance proxy from the Parkinson volatility estimator, estimates the discretized Heston variance process by quasi-maximum likelihood estimation (QMLE), and derives a theory-based benchmark return from the conditional mean of log returns; a convolutional neural network (CNN) then learns, over rolling windows, the nonlinear residual of realized returns relative to this benchmark. Using 10,019 daily WTI crude oil futures prices from 2 January 1986 to 12 May 2025, the hybrid model attains an out-of-sample R² of at least 0.9895 and a MAPE of about 1.82% across rolling windows of 30–180 days, outperforming CNN, RNN, BP, SVR, MLP and the other Heston-based hybrid models with markedly smaller error variability. Backtests further show that the forecasts carry economic value in a simple timing strategy, indicating that coupling financial theory with deep learning is a viable route for energy price forecasting.
why: Commodity price forecaster with theory grounding; unclear out-of-sample rigor.

title: Equity Signals and Mortgage-Backed Security Returns: An AI-Agent-Assisted Systematic Meta-Analysis
abstract: Published estimates of how equity market signals relate to mortgage-backed security outcomes differ in sign across otherwise similar specifications. We assemble these scattered coefficients through an AI-agent-assisted systematic review in which the agent performs retrieval, screening, and extraction while a finance domain expert holds exclusive authority over every coefficient and classification judgment. Screening yields ten confirmed estimates from two studies. The apparent disagreement resolves into a moderator: the benchmark asset against which the MBS convenience premium is measured determines the sign of the volatility effect. Within one baseline regression, a one-point increase in VIX raises the premium measured against AAA corporate bonds by 3.207 basis points and lowers the premium measured against Treasury securities by 1.257, both significant at the 1% level. Because estimates measured against different benchmarks belong to different strata, we report no pooled effect size. We have identified no comparable synthesis of this literature.
why: AI-assisted meta-analysis on equity-MBS relations; limited scope, two studies.

title: Federated Transfer Learning for SME Credit Risk using BayesShield and Paillier Encryption
abstract: The assessment of credit risk for Small and Medium-sized Enterprises (SMEs) presents a significant challenge in the financial sector, primarily due to these entities' characteristic lack of extensive credit histories and reliance on non-standardized, alternative data. Traditional machine learning models are often ineffective in this sparse data environment, and the fragmented nature of SME data across various financial institutions prevents the development of robust, centralized models due to stringent data privacy regulations. This research proposes a novel framework that synergistically combines Federated Transfer Learning (FTL), a privacy-preserving Bayesian neural network (BayesShield), and Paillier homomorphic encryption to address these dual challenges of data scarcity and privacy. The FTL architecture enables collaborative model training across multiple institutions without the need for raw data exchange, leveraging knowledge from a data-rich source domain (e.g., large corporate credit data) to enhance learning in a data-scarce target domain (SME credit risk). To manage the inherent uncertainty in SME financials and provide well-calibrated risk probabilities, the framework integrates BayesShield, a Bayesian neural network that offers robust uncertainty quantification and is resilient to adversarial attacks. Crucially, the security of the entire collaborative learning process is fortified by the integration of Paillier encryption, a fully homomorphic encryption scheme that allows for mathematical operations on ciphertexts. This ensures that all intermediate model updates, gradients, and parameters exchanged during the federated process remain encrypted, preventing any potential information leakage to malicious adversaries or even the central server. By integrating these advanced techniques, our proposed framework not only enhances the predictive accuracy and reliability of SME credit scoring but also establishes a new standard for secure, privacy-preserving collaborative finance, enabling financial inclusion while rigorously complying with data protection regulations such as GDPR and CCPA.
why: Framework proposal (FTL+BayesShield), no data, results, or evidence.

title: The limits of price-based coordination in electricity market design: A multi-criteria agent-based benchmark of eight competing architectures
abstract: As the electrification of heating and mobility accelerates, activating demand-side flexibility is critical to preventing distribution grid congestion, yet the comparative impacts of competing market architectures remain contested. This study presents the first agent-based comparison of this breadth: eight competing market designs, from flat tariffs to local energy markets, simulated under identical conditions on a future high-flexibility German low-voltage feeder used as a forward-looking stress test. The central finding is a structural complexity-performance paradox. Increasing market sophistication does not produce monotonic performance improvements across technical, economic, social, and environmental dimensions. Deploying a home energy management system under static tariffs already captures a substantial local optimization dividend. Conversely, dynamic pricing improves economic and environmental outcomes but worsens grid stress through load synchronization, driving peak transformer loading above 400 % of rated capacity. Feeder-level dynamic grid fees struggle to prevent these overloads, while local energy markets offer a more balanced profile but cannot resolve structural winter congestion. Benchmarked against a constrained-optimum reference whose dual is the distribution locational marginal price, the price-based designs sit far from a coordination that secures the feeder at its rating, exposing their overloads as a coordination artifact rather than a physical capacity deficit. The underlying mechanism is the inability of pure energy-price signals to substitute for instantaneous, locational capacity coordination, indicating that grid-compatible operation depends on enforcing the transfer-capacity constraint rather than approximating it through a price.
why: Agent-based market simulation well-executed; electricity domain, not financial markets.

title: AI Empowerment, Supply Chain Transmission, and Firm Carbon Emission Volatility
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping firms' production organization and supply chain governance structures. However, its environmental consequences extend beyond changes in the level of carbon emissions to encompass the stability of emission trajectories. Using the staggered establishment of National Pilot Zones for New-Generation Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Development as a quasi-natural experiment, and drawing on supply chain-matched panel data of Chinese A-share listed firms from 2010 to 2023, this paper constructs a staggered difference-indifferences (DID) design to examine how AI empowerment among midstream core (anchor) firms affects the carbon emission volatility of their upstream suppliers and downstream customers. We find that after the cities hosting midstream core firms are designated as AI pilot zones, the carbon emission volatility of upstream suppliers declines significantly, while that of downstream customers rises significantly-an asymmetric transmission pattern of "dampening upstream volatility while amplifying downstream volatility." Further tests provide evidence consistent with the view that trade credit arrangements, operating expense adjustments, and changes in financing constraints are important channels through which AI empowerment affects supply chain carbon emission volatility, while the digital infrastructure of supply chain firms and the intensity of industry competition constitute important boundary conditions for this effect. This paper advances research on the environmental effects of AI from emission levels to emission volatility and uncovers a mechanism of carbon risk redistribution along the supply chain amid digital transformation.
why: Empirical AI adoption impact on emissions; single-country, limited generalization.

title: From Social Media Data to Customer Insights: AI-Based Gender Profiling in Polish Financial Discourse
abstract: The study examines how social media data can generate customer insight by identifying gender-related patterns in Polish financial discourse. We analyze 77,098 posts collected from X. A linguistic heuristic labeled 810 posts by women and 2,427 by men. Iterative labeling then expanded the training data using Polish BERT, HerBERT, and XLM-RoBERTa, alongside embeddings from Polish BERT, Bielik, DeepSeek, and OpenAI classified with conventional machine-learning algorithms. DeepSeek and OpenAI embeddings combined with Support Vector Machines and Logistic Regression achieved approximately 99% accuracy across training, test, and validation sets. LIME-based interpretation revealed differences in financial themes associated with women's and men's discourse. The findings demonstrate that domain-specific language analytics can support audience understanding, communication design, and personalization in financial services, while multilingual embeddings may outperform language-specific models in local contexts. Because inferred gender is sensitive and the corpus is platform-specific, results should support segment-level research and message evaluation, not individual decisions.
why: Polish financial discourse gender analysis; social science slant, limited actionability.

title: AI-Driven RegTech Compliance Frameworks: Mitigating Regulatory Risk for Fintech in Underserved U.S. Markets
abstract: Fintech companies serving underserved segments of the U.S. financial system operate under a compliance burden that is disproportionate to their size and structurally difficult to manage with conventional methods. These institutions must satisfy the same anti-money laundering, consumer protection, and fair lending obligations as large depository institutions, while working with thinner compliance staffing, less mature risk infrastructure, and customer populations that are harder to evaluate through traditional underwriting and identityverification tools. This article examines how artificial intelligence-driven regulatory technology (RegTech) can be structured to reduce regulatory risk in this environment, and proposes a risk-management framework that draws on methodologies developed in high-volume litigation risk assessment. Litigation risk management and regulatory compliance share a common analytical structure: both require the triage of large volumes of variable-quality information under time and resource constraints, the early identification of exposure before it becomes unmanageable, and documentation practices that must withstand external scrutiny. The article argues that AI-driven compliance systems are most effective, and most defensible before regulators, when they are built around this triage-anddocumentation logic rather than around prediction accuracy alone. The article reviews the current regulatory and technological landscape, identifies the principal risk areas for fintech firms operating in underserved markets, and sets out a four-component compliance framework: risk-tiered monitoring, explainable decisioning, adverse-action documentation, and supervisory-ready audit trails. The article concludes that the most significant barrier to effective AIdriven compliance is not technical capability but the absence of documentation and explainability practices adequate to satisfy examiners and courts, and that closing this gap is where the greatest near-term value lies.
why: RegTech compliance framework; position paper without clear implementation path.

title: AI Pricing Algorithms and the Risk of Tacit Collusion: Assessing Competition Law Response
abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in corporate pricing has raised con cerns about its impact on competition, particularly within oligopolistic industries. The paper examines whether AI driven pricing algorithms increase the risk of tacit collusion and whether existing competition law frameworks are adequately equipped to address this challenge from a law and economics perspective. AI pricing algo rithms can improve firms’ efficiency by processing market data, responding rapidly to competitors, and adjusting prices dynamically. However, these same capabilities may allow firms to sustain higher prices and more stable profit margins without direct communication or human intent. This can intensify traditional market fail ures, including reduced consumer surplus and allocative inefficiency. Drawing on competition law frameworks in the European Union, the United Kingdom, and the United States, this paper finds that AI pricing algorithms increase the likelihood and stability of tacit collusion. Moreover, it finds that current legal doctrines, built around agreement and intentional coordination, only partially capture this risk. More proportionate responses, such as enhanced monitoring, targeted burden shift ing in concentrated markets, and guidance on algorithm design, may prove more effective than broad prohibitions.
why: Legal framework analysis on collusion risk, not technical method or dataset.

title: Legal and Ethical Challenges of AI-Driven Insurance Fraud Detection in the United States
abstract: American insurers now screen a large share of first notices of loss through machine learning models that assign each claim a probability of fraud. The technology answers a real problem: fraud is estimated to drain more than $300 billion from the United States economy each year, and generative image tools have made fabricated evidence cheap enough for ordinary claimants to produce. But the architecture that makes these systems efficient also makes them legally exposed and ethically fraught. A fraud score is an accusation rendered in probability, generated from correlations the insurer often cannot fully explain, applied to a population in which genuine fraud is rare, and enforced through delay and demands for documentation rather than formal denial. This paper examines that tension across four fraud archetypes false injury claims, inflated medical bills, staged accidents and identity fraud and maps the governing legal terrain: state insurance regulation under the McCarran-Ferguson framework, the NAIC Model Bulletin and its state analogues, unfair claims settlement practices statutes and bad faith doctrine, antidiscrimination law, privacy and biometric statutes, and the Fair Credit Reporting Act. It then addresses questions law has not resolved: the base rate problem, proxy discrimination, automation bias in nominal human review, surveillance creep, and the structural conflict between fraud control and cost containment. Drawing on pending litigation in Huskey v State Farm and Estate of Lokken v UnitedHealth Group, the paper argues that the decisive question is not whether insurers may use AI to detect fraud they plainly may, and arguably must but whether the claimant burdened by an algorithmic suspicion retains a meaningful capacity to contest it.
why: Insurance fraud legal/ethical challenges analyzed; no implementable technical contribution.

title: Improving Financial Cybersecurity Through Fraud Transaction with Deep Learning-Based Advanced Models
abstract: The quick digitalization of financial services has greatly exposed financial operations to cyber threats. Conventional rule-based cybersecurity controls do not have the strength to protect against the changing attack schemes, such as fraud, identity theft, adversarial manipulation, and advanced persistent threats. The research presents a deep learning-based approach to detect fraudulent transactions by using the Fraud Detection Transactions Dataset. The proposed solution includes a large amount of data preparation, such as outlier detection, feature engineering, label encoding, feature scaling, and class imbalance control with SMOTE. There are two types of categorization models: artificial neural networks (ANNs) and wide-and-deep neural networks. Experimental results show that the Wide & Deep model outperforms the ANN in acc (0.9846), prec (0.9634), rec (0.9895), F1-score (0.9763), and ROC-AUC (0.99). Fraud patterns of complex nature can be detected by the linear and DL elements. In addition, an ablation study is applied to show the effects of the various optimizers, and their comparison with the current models proves the power of the developed approach. The results demonstrate that cybersecurity systems for financial transactions may greatly benefit from using the Wide and Deep architecture to enhance the precision and resilience of fraud detection.
why: Standard fraud detection pipeline; no novelty, template approach.

title: Stock Price Prediction using Hybrid Deep Learning: Evidence from Thailand's Equity Market
abstract: This study examines whether the internal configuration of hybrid deep learning architectures influences stock price forecasting performance. Six models are evaluated using daily prices of 18 SET50 stocks in Thailand from July 2019 to July 2024: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN)-LSTM, and four Conditional Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Network with Gradient Penalty (CWGAN-GP) configurations employing different generator and discriminator architectures. Forecasting performance is assessed using price-level error metrics and directional measures. The results show that CNN-LSTM-CWGAN-GP, which employs a CNN generator and LSTM discriminator, provides the strongest price-level forecasting performance, achieving the lowest RMSE, MAE, and MAPE for 14 of the 18 stocks. However, superiority in price-level accuracy does not translate directly into directional forecasting performance. CWGAN-GP achieves the highest directional accuracy for seven stocks, while CWGAN-GP and LSTM-CWGAN-GP each achieve the highest F1score for five stocks. These findings demonstrate that forecasting performance depends on both the allocation of neural components within the adversarial architecture and the forecasting objective. The study provides evidence that hybrid adversarial configurations differ substantially in their relative forecasting performance, while highlighting the importance of evaluating price-level accuracy and directional performance separately.
why: Thai stock predictor; no transaction costs, out-of-sample discipline.

title: The Human Capital Gap: Institutional Readiness for AI-Driven Labor Market Transformation in Emerging Economies
abstract: This book proposes and operationalizes the Skills Transition Readiness Index (STRI), a four-dimension framework — labor-market institutional flexibility, human capital stock and skill composition, AI adoption capacity, and transition/social protection mechanisms — for measuring institutional readiness for AI-driven labor-market transformation. Distinct from existing AI-readiness instruments, which rely on pooled cross-country regression, the book specifies a selection-corrected, heterogeneous-treatment-effect econometric strategy, in the applied microeconometric tradition of Heckman, Vytlacil, and Urzúa's work on selection models with heterogeneity, for estimating how the returns to cognitive and non-cognitive skills shift under AI exposure. The volume includes a full operationalization table, structural equations for the composite index, a comparative illustration across Latin America and Central-Eastern Europe using verified World Bank Human Capital Index data, and an executable specification for the companion empirical volume (worker-level estimation, robustness battery, and PCA-weight sensitivity checks). Part of "The Gap" institutional-readiness book series. License: CC-BY 4.0. ORCID: 0009-0007-8558-164X. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22795764.
why: Labor market policy analysis; not directly implementable for practitioners.

title: Governing Artificial Intelligence in Finance: Strategies for Balancing Sustainable Development, Innovation, Risk, and Competitiveness
abstract: This research paper is written by Douglas W. Arner ( University of Hong Kong/University of Cambridge/Queen Mary University of London ) and Christine Menglu Wang ( National University of Singapore ). The rapid development and increasing accessibility of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are transforming finance. In many respects, the financial sector has led AI use (in some cases, for over two decades), not least in the context of trading and risk-management activities. Financial institutions are accelerating AI adoption to increase operational efficiency, improve risk management, and enhance their business activities. In terms of risk management, regulatory compliance, and supervisory monitoring, AI is already being widely used by both industry and regulators, improving the soundness and safety of financial markets. However, the increasing use of AI exposes the financial sector to a range of challenges and risks. In this paper, we analyse approaches to AI governance in finance. Following an analysis of the use of AI in finance, we first present a new taxonomy of governance and regulatory approaches based on a framework of five main elements: strategy, approach, scope, framework, and technology, derived from analysis of evolving practices across the world. Second, we develop a new analytical framework and taxonomy for the major categories of AI risk and governance across five main risk areas: macro risks, micro or sectoral risks, infrastructure risks, malicious actor and behaviour risks, and culture and human capital risks. We conclude the paper by framing the core elements of strategic approaches in terms of the development and governance of AI in finance, based on these twin taxonomies, focusing on strategy, infrastructure, regulatory approaches, the use of technology for regulatory and supervisory purposes, and the importance of developing the wider ecosystem.
why: AI finance governance and policy analysis; not technical.

title: Learning Externalities and Price Discrimination in LLM Markets
abstract: Large-language-model (LLM) providers commonly offer subscriptions whose marginal usage price can fall below marginal inference cost, even though users differ substantially in what they cost to serve. This paper studies a countervailing force: intensive users generate training-relevant interactions that improve subsequent model quality. In a two-period model, casual and power users differ only in their marginal contribution to future model quality, while enterprise users benefit from quality improvements but contractually exclude their data from training. The provider optimally discounts contributing users in proportion to their learning value. Under linear pricing, price discrimination raises both terminal quality and total surplus relative to uniform pricing, since the static allocation distortion is second-order relative to the dynamic gain. However, the level of learning is inefficient, because the provider's marginal return to higher quality is smaller than the marginal social return; consumers appropriate the remaining return in their period-2 consumer surplus. A two-part tariff enables the provider to appropriate that surplus in full, achieving the first-best allocation and predicting the observed pattern in which high-contribution users pay more in total and less per unit.
why: LLM pricing economics theory; no empirical validation or actionability.

title: Innovation and Miscalibration of Expectations: Between Economic Growth and Financial Instability
abstract: Technological innovation is an important source of long-term economic growth. At the same time, periods of rapid technological change have frequently coincided with investment booms, and, in some cases, severe financial instability. This paper argues that financial instability may arise when economic decision makers systematically miscalibrate their expectations concerning the innovation. We argue that two related but analytically distinct behavioral mechanisms operate simultaneously. Corporate decision makers overestimate future demand, market size, market share, and the persistence of high returns, leading to excessive investment and ultimately declining marginal profitability. Investors, in turn, may correctly anticipate the long-run transformative potential of a technology while capitalizing its expected benefits too early in current asset prices. Narrative biases and herding synchronize these errors, reinforcing both investment and valuation dynamics. Building on insights from macroeconomics, financial instability theory, and behavioral finance, the paper develops a theoretical framework linking innovation, expectations, corporate investment, asset prices, competition, declining marginal returns, leverage, and financial correction. Historical episodes including the British Railway Mania, the U.S. railroad boom, the Roaring Twenties and Great Depression, the Asian Financial Crisis, and the Internet and telecommunications bubble are used to illustrate the mechanism. Artificial intelligence is then considered as a contemporary test of the framework. The central implication is that an innovation can be simultaneously genuine, economically transformative, and financially overvalued in the short run. A financial crisis may therefore represent not the failure of an innovation, but the correction of expectations concerning the timing, speed, distribution, and profitability of its economic realization.
why: Innovation miscalibration theory; no data or testable mechanism.

title: Prediction, Configuration and Endogenous Demand Iain M. Banks's Culture and the Demand Side of AI-Mediated Planning
abstract: Artificial intelligence has reopened the socialist calculation debate by weakening constraints once treated as fixed. This paper uses Iain M. Banks's Culture as an institutional thought experiment to ask what follows when prediction can substitute for some transfers of local knowledge. The argument turns on configuration. Prediction matters little for goods that can simply be supplied on request, but more where capacity or shared environments must be set in advance. In those cases, acting on predicted demand can help shape the preferences later observed. Realised demand may then fit more than one account of how those preferences formed, and durable configuration may make some comparisons difficult to recover. The Culture holds together powerful but fallible machine prediction, protected interiority, marginal abundance, configurational constraints, polycentric agency and exit. It therefore clarifies both what AI may weaken in the knowledge problem and what remains difficult on the demand side of planning.
why: Theoretical thought experiment on prediction; no data or implementation path.

title: Pricing AI Technology for Healthcare Services
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can improve healthcare quality and service throughput, but greater AI capability does not necessarily mean more patients receive AI-assisted care. We consider a game-theoretic queueing model of the interactions among AI firm pricing, hospital adoption and capacity decisions, and patients' care-seeking decisions. The AI firm sells an AI tool to a hospital. The tool's AI capability is characterized by its effectiveness in improving care quality and efficiency in increasing service rate. The firm chooses among subscription, pay-per-use, and hybrid pricing. Each AI use generates data value and incurs an operating cost, and their difference is the firm's net value per AI use. We obtain three main results. First, although AI is often expected to substitute for clinical labor, the hospital may expand capacity after AI adoption when demand expansion from improved quality and throughput dominates efficiency gains that reduce capacity requirements. Second, AI adoption does not necessarily increase the number of patients served relative to the no-AI benchmark. AI penetration, measured by the number of patients receiving AI-assisted care, is highest under subscription and lowest under pay-per-use pricing. Third, subscription pricing is optimal when the firm's net value per AI use is nonnegative. When it is negative, the optimal scheme may shift from pay-per-use to hybrid or subscription pricing as AI efficiency increases. The thresholds decrease as AI effectiveness improves. Pay-per-use pricing can create a win-win outcome for the hospital and AI firm yet need not expand patient access.
why: Healthcare economics game theory; wrong domain, pure theory.

title: Leveraging Machine Learning & Artificial Intelligence for Financial Fraud Detection: Datasets, Gaps & Analyst Implications
abstract: Financial fraud is now among the most serious threats to global financial systems. Reported losses in the United States alone exceeded $12.5 billion in 2024 [1]. Rule-based detection, long the industry default, is steadily losing ground to fraud schemes that adapt faster than the rules meant to catch them [4, 8]. This paper surveys how Machine Learning (ML) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) are currently applied to financial fraud detection, with attention to the resources and skills that matter for Data Analyst and Financial Analyst roles. We review seven publicly available datasets [9, 10] and set out six research gaps supported by 2025-2026 literature. We also draw on work from adjacent fields: AI-driven cybersecurity threat detection [13], hybrid phishing detection [14], AI-powered software defect prediction [15], structural bias auditing in security systems [16], deep learning for malware classification and threat intelligence in hospital environments [28], and explainable AI for trust and transparency in financial security systems [27]. Read together, these domains share a recurring set of problems: class imbalance, limited model explainability, concept drift, and regulatory compliance, all of which apply squarely to fraud detection [17, 18, 22]. We link these themes to what analysts actually do day to day, and close with a career-oriented roadmap.
why: Survey of fraud-detection ML (explicitly rejected category).

title: Artificial Intelligence in Business Research: A Synthesis of Accounting, Finance, and Management
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) refers to a set of computational techniques, including machine learning, natural language processing, deep learning, and generative AI, that enable systems to perform tasks traditionally requiring human intelligence, such as prediction, pattern recognition, and decision-making. The rapid diffusion of AI into business organizations is transforming how information is processed, decisions are made, and knowledge-intensive work is performed, creating both new opportunities for economic value and new challenges for human judgment, organizational governance, and accountability. The growing adoption of AI across accounting, finance, and management makes it increasingly important to understand not only what AI can do, but also how and under what conditions it affects individuals, organizations, and markets. This paper provides a comprehensive review of the rapidly growing literature on artificial intelligence across these three disciplines. We synthesize existing research to examine how AI is transforming information processing, decision-making, governance, and organizational performance. In accounting, AI enhances auditing, financial reporting, and fraud detection while raising concerns regarding transparency and professional judgment. In finance, AI improves asset pricing, risk assessment, and trading strategies by leveraging large-scale structured and unstructured data. In management, AI reshapes organizational design, human capital, strategic decision-making, and innovation through increasingly sophisticated human–AI collaboration. Across these disciplines, we organize the literature around several unifying themes, including information asymmetry, automation versus augmentation, decision quality, interpretability, and governance. We further identify important research gaps concerning whether AI’s predictive and analytical advantages translate into meaningful economic and organizational outcomes, how AI reshapes human judgment and skills, the emerging risks, and the need for stronger research designs. By integrating evidence across three major business disciplines, this review provides a unified framework for understanding AI’s transformative role in organizations and offers a roadmap for future interdisciplinary research on the economic, behavioral, organizational, and governance consequences of AI.
why: Comprehensive AI literature review; explicitly rejected format.

title: Powering Intelligence - Europe, the UK & the Middle East : A Regional Analysis of Electricity Economics, Climate Advantage, Innovation Tax Incentives, Regulatory Risk and Institutional Integrity for AI Data-Center Investment
abstract: This report benchmarks electricity cost and generation mix across 31 European markets (the EU-27, the UK, Norway, Switzerland, and Iceland) and five Middle Eastern markets, and introduces the EMEA AI Power & Innovation Competitiveness Index (“PCI-EMEA”) across the 20 countries most active in AI infrastructure siting. Six weighted components drive the Index: electricity cost, climate and cooling advantage, water stress, an illustrative tax position, regulatory and grid risk, and, new in this edition, an Institutional Integrity / Public-Sector Corruption Proxy (CPI) measured by Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index. Every component is built from a named external source or a stated, checkable formula (Section 2); the Index is best described as externally benchmarked and transparently modeled, not as an infallible ranking, and Section 2 states plainly where inputs are directly observed versus analyst-estimated. PCI-EMEA is a country-screening tool, not a site-selection model: a strong national score narrows the field worth investigating, it does not certify that any specific site, substation, or parcel of land within that country is suitable. Constructability in particular is not scored here (Section 2.7, Section 8.5). On tax: Ireland's R&D credit rose from 30% to 35% in Budget 2026 and is structured as a qualifying refundable credit; per HMRC guidance, the UK's RDEC is also treated as qualifying-refundable. Both are treated as qualifying refundable tax credits for purposes of the simplified model and therefore are not subject to the same 15% cash-tax floor applied here to non-QRTCs, but only Ireland's is large enough, relative to the illustrative company's R&D intensity, to produce a negative modeled cash-tax position; the UK's produces a positive, if reduced, one. Several other governments, Finland, Denmark, Portugal, Poland, and Italy among them, do operate real R&D incentives of their own (Section 5.1), but structured as ordinary deductions or non-refundable credits, which the Pillar Two floor neutralizes to the same 15% outcome once a company is large enough to be in scope. Five years ago, “which country has the lowest corporate tax rate” was close to the whole conversation. It no longer is, and increasingly, neither is “which country has an R&D credit”; what matters is whether that credit is refundable, and how large it is relative to what the company actually spends. On regulation: the EU AI Act's high-risk system obligations, originally due 2 August 2026, were pushed to 2 December 2027 by a “Digital Omnibus” that entered into force on 27 July 2026. Article 50's transparency obligations apply from 2 August 2026, subject to the limited transition for Article 50(2) machine-readable marking described below: the disclosure obligations under Article 50(1), (3), (4), and (5), covering direct human-AI interaction, emotion-recognition/biometric-categorisation disclosure, deepfake and AI-generated public-interest text labelling, and how those disclosures must be presented, carry no grace period and are enforceable from that date. Only the machine-readable marking duty under Article 50(2) carries a narrow four-month grace period, to 2 December 2026, for generative systems already on the market before 2 August 2026 [18]. “The EU delayed the AI Act” is true only for the high-risk tier. On Ireland specifically: data centres consumed approximately 23% of Ireland's metered national electricity in 2025, per the Central Statistics Office, up from 5% in 2015. The grid-connection framework that replaced the country's 2021-2025 de facto moratorium applies a tiered set of obligations from a 1 MVA de minimis threshold, with the largest projects, 10 MVA and above, required to provide dispatchable generation or storage covering the full extent of their maximum import capacity on a derated basis, and all qualifying projects required to match at least 80% of annual demand with additional Irish renewable electricity. That framework is real and binding, but newly implemented and not yet tested by a full construction cycle, which is why Ireland's regulatory-risk score remains the second-lowest in the set even as its tax position is the strongest.
why: Data center electricity benchmarking; infrastructure analysis, not LLM system building.

title: Islamic Banking and the Sabbath Pond Test: A Re-Evaluation through Classical Islamic Economic Sources
abstract: This paper re-examines the practices of modern Islamic banking through the lens of classical Islamic economic principles. By applying what we term the “Sabbath Pond Test”—a metaphor drawn from the Qur’anic account of a community that circumvented the prohibition on fishing on the Sabbath—we assess whether contemporary Islamic financial products avoid the substance of riba (usury) or merely its form. Drawing on Qur’anic injunctions, Prophetic Hadith, and Hanafi jurisprudence (including works like Ahkam al-Qur’an, Kitab al-Amwal, Kitab al-Kharaj, and Usul al-Shashi), the paper critically analyzes a hypothetical case study of an Islamic mortgage structure that imitates an interest-bearing loan via sale, lease, and buy-back arrangements. We then present classical, interest-free financing alternatives such as Musharakah and Mudarabah, as well as public finance measures from early Islamic history that prioritized risk-sharing and social welfare. The study finds that while Islamic banks like Meezan Bank claim Sharī‘ah compliance by contract technicalities, there is an urgent need for greater transparency and alignment with the maqasid (objectives) of Sharī‘ah — emphasizing justice and economic substance over form. AI Assistance Disclosure: Claude (Anthropic) and ChatGPT (OpenAI) were used for language refinement, paraphrasing, structural editing, clarity improvements, formatting and citation-style consistency checks, preliminary source discovery and citation suggestions, and translation into other languages. The idea of applying the Sabbath Pond analogy to contemporary Islamic banking originated with the author. The author is accountable for the manuscript’s content; no AI tool is credited as an author. Academic preprint; not a fatwa or financial advice. Archived at Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21545850. Web edition: https://irshados.com/ebooks/islamic-banking-sabbath-pond-test-reevaluation/
why: Islamic banking jurisprudence; off-topic theology, no financial relevance.

title: A Data-light Bottom-up Framework for Urban Building-Stocks Retrofit Screening: Integrating locally Adapted Computer Vision with Multi-Source Data
abstract: City-scale retrofit programs require often unavailable or impractical to collect building-level information, especially at scale. This study presents a data-light framework integrating RGB-based indoor temperature prediction, building-feature extraction, EnergyPlus-based Bayesian calibration, and LLM-assisted reporting for bottom-up preliminary envelope assessment. RGB-based temperature prediction achieved an MAE of 0.54°C on optimal training-test distributions, while locally adapted visual models achieved over 80% test accuracy for several building categorical features and an MAE of 11.9 years for building age. A four-zone case study further showed that integrating these information sources with physics-based calibration could translate them into differentiated envelope and retrofit assessments, including among multiple zones within the same building. Overall, the framework is not a substitute for an investment-grade audit; instead, it provides a pathway for combining local observations with physics-based models to prioritize practical diagnostics and retrofit action within urban building stocks.
why: Building retrofit computer vision; off-topic real estate, no finance.
